extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Examining Corps / patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO examination guidance for analyzing subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 for claims that recite or involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, natural principles, and/or natural products. Provides a three-question flow, a factor-based "significantly different" test, examples, and a rejection form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall three-question process for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in accordance with MPEP §2103, walk through the three questions in the flowchart to determine whether the claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not eligible at any stage, the claim is prima facie ineligible and should be rejected using revised form paragraph 7.05.13. Use MPEP §2103 for claim interpretation; state all non-cumulative reasons in the first Office action under compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 1: Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claimed invention directed to one of the four statutory patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. See MPEP §706.03 for appropriate form paragraphs. Note: claims to humans per se are not directed to statutory subject matter (AIA Section 33(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 2: Judicial exception present?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, and natural products)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, claim is patent-eligible. If yes, or unclear, proceed to Question 3. Examples of natural products include chemicals derived from nature (antibiotics, fats, oils, etc.), foods, metals/minerals, natural materials (rocks, soils), nucleic acids, organisms, proteins/peptides, and substances found in or derived from nature. If in doubt that claim recites something similar to a natural product, proceed to Question 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 3: Claim as a whole significantly different?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites an abstract idea, analyze using MPEP §2106(II) only. Otherwise, perform the factor-based analysis in Part II. If the totality of relevant factors indicates the claim is not significantly different, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 using revised form paragraph 7.05.13; if it is significantly different, the claim is patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of MPEP §2106(II) for abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no change to examination of claims reciting an abstract idea; they should continue to be analyzed for subject matter eligibility using the existing guidance in MPEP §2106(II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites an abstract idea (even if combined with other judicial exceptions), do not apply the factor-based 'significantly different' analysis here; follow MPEP §2106(II) guidance, including evaluation of practical application factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor-based analysis: totality and weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the listed factors (a–l) to analyze whether the claim as a whole is 'significantly different' than the judicial exception; weigh the totality of relevant factors. The weight accorded each factor varies with the facts; consider every relevant factor and related evidence before concluding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On balance, if the totality of relevant factors weighs toward eligibility, the claim qualifies; if against, the claim should be rejected. Not every factor will be relevant to every claim. This approach is analogous to the Wands undue-experimentation analysis (MPEP 2164.01(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a) product claim markedly different
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that initially appears to be a natural product, but after analysis is determined to be non-naturally occurring and markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To satisfy, identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring products and evaluate whether those differences together rise to the level of a marked difference in structure. Not all changes (e.g., mere isolation) rise to marked differences. Marked differences may be structural and/or functional; being produced by routine manipulation does not preclude weighing toward eligibility (e.g., cDNA, hybrid plants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor b) meaningful limits on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that impose meaningful limits on claim scope, i.e., the elements/steps narrow the scope of the claim so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: specific dosages, time frames, patient types, or other limitations that confine use to a particular application. If elements meaningfully limit scope, they weigh toward eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor c) elements significantly related to the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that relate to the judicial exception in a significant way, i.e., the elements/steps are more than nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related to the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that integrate, manipulate or materially change the judicial exception (not merely mention it) favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor d) more than general instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that do more than describe the judicial exception(s) with general instructions to apply or use the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that only include high-level instructions to apply a natural principle weigh against eligibility; concrete, specific steps weigh toward eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor e) particular machine or transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that include a particular machine or transformation of a particular article, where the particular machine/transformation implements one or more judicial exception(s) or integrates the judicial exception(s) into a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106(II)(B)(1) for explanation of machine-or-transformation factors. A specific machine/transformation that meaningfully integrates the exception favors eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor f) more than well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites one or more elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that add a feature that is more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements perform non-routine functions or are themselves novel/non-conventional, they weigh toward eligibility. Prior routine use of components for different purposes does not automatically make the claim conventional for the claimed application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor g) product claim not markedly different
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that appears to be a natural product that is not markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited product is structurally (and functionally) not markedly different from its natural counterpart, this factor weighs against eligibility (e.g., purified product structurally identical to natural form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor h) high-level generality covering all practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception(s) are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims drafted so broadly that they foreclose substantially all uses of the natural principle/product weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor i) elements required to apply the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements dictate how others must perform the exception (i.e., are effectively required to practice it), this weighs against eligibility; if alternatives exist, this factor may not be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor j) additional elements are well-understood, conventional, routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the extra elements are routine/conventional in the relevant art, they are unlikely to render the claim significantly different and weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor k) insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are insignificant extra-solution activity, e.g., are merely appended to the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely tacking on trivial activities that do not meaningfully integrate the exception or confine its use should not render the claim eligible; such activity weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor l) mere field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that amount to nothing more than a mere field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting use of a judicial exception to a particular field or environment without adding substantive limitations is insufficient to make the claim significantly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marked-difference inquiry (Chakrabarty-centered)
rubrics_metrics.description: For natural products, analyze whether the claimed product is a non-naturally occurring product of human ingenuity that is 'markedly different' from naturally occurring products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad reaffirmed reliance on Chakrabarty's criterion: identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring counterparts, then evaluate whether differences together rise to a marked structural difference. Mere recitation of words like 'isolated' or routine manipulation may not create a marked difference. Structural differences that also produce functional differences strengthen the case for marked difference (e.g., chemically modified molecules, cDNA, engineered organisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: When factors are not relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every factor (a–l) will be relevant to every claim and need not be considered in every analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim drawn solely to a nucleic acid will generally only implicate factors a) and g). Examiners should identify which factors apply given the claim's content and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other statutory provisions and compact prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses a judicial exception such as a natural product, sections 102, 103, and 112 provide additional tools for ensuring patentability. Under principles of compact prosecution, Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should include non-redundant rejections under other statutes where appropriate to provide a complete prima facie case of unpatentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 usage and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 should be used when rejecting claims that recite or involve a law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 2 of the paragraph, identify the judicial exception(s) recited or involved and explain why the element(s)/step(s) in addition to the judicial exception(s) do not result in the claim as a whole reciting something significantly different. Explain why the claim features do not add significantly more and/or fail to show a marked difference; show why features are extra-solution activity, mere field-of-use, or conventional/routine. The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case.
